items.originalTitle: ‘Grandfather’ or ‘godfather’? Republicans know they’re stuck with Trump
items.author: Andrew Howard and Aaron Pellish
items.title: ‘Grandfather’ or ‘godfather’? Republicans know they’re stuck with Trump
items.summary: Republican leaders grappling with how to recover after their devastating midterm losses agree on one thing: President Donald Trump isn't going anywhere in 2028, even if some wish he would. Interviews with more than two dozen GOP state and county officials from red, blue and purple states across the country conducted since Election Day revealed a party still processing their election drubbing and at a loss for how to move forward. Some want to move on from Trump entirely. Some are eager for his involvement. And others are just resigned that he’s going to do whatever he wants, regardless of their preferences. All of them are worried about the party’s chances of retaining control of the White House in two short years, but they also recognize its current occupant is going to continue to exercise a huge role in the future of the party. “President Trump is going to be part of it, whether we want that or not,” said Arkansas GOP chair Joseph Wood. “His voters are still going to be Republicans that we need to have come out in this election in two years.” That leaves the party in a precarious position. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found the president’s approval rating at 32% overall, and at 70% among Republicans — down from 91% on inauguration day last year. A POLITICO Poll taken after the midterms found 56% of Trump’s 2024 voters believe the Republican Party needs to distance itself from him and his agenda. But no one in the party expects that to happen. And Trump has already taken steps to maintain his grip on the GOP, endorsing Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters for another term and ordering his powerful super PAC to continue fundraising ahead of 2028. A handful of Republican grassroots leaders were openly critical of Trump. “I don't know how much he really has to offer,” said Vermont GOP chair Paul Dame. “I think most people are ready to move on in a new direction.” Added Michael Bub, the chair of ruby-red Taylor County, Wisconsin, Republican Party :“He should stay out of it. Look at the people he endorsed: They lost.” In a statement, RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassare said “President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party.” “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our voters and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win in 2028,” she said. The White House demurred, pointing to the RNC’s response. Many party officials are resigned to Trump doing whatever he wants, given his domineering personality and strong sway over the party base. Nebraska Republican Party Chair Mary Jane Truemper said “Donald Trump's going to play whatever role he wants to play.” “He's the president,” Truemper said. “I look at things as they are and not as I want them to be.” That’s leaving some state-level Republican leaders wanting the president to take on a more constructive role and be willing to let other candidates and ideas rise. “I hope he becomes kind of the mentor grandfather, and not the godfather,” said Kansas GOP chair Danedri Herbert. “In America, we hope and expect our presidents to not keep a tight grip on the party, to recognize that now it's time for me to mentor the next generation.” Added outgoing Minnesota Republican Party Chair Alex Plechash: “We need to capitalize on what he brought to the party and do what we can to retain that. But there has been a definite turn in the political landscape.” Virtually every GOP official cited the poor political environment caused in part by the president’s handling of the economy and the war in Iran as the reason for the party’s midterm meltdown. But many stopped short of laying the blame directly at the president’s feet, a sign of how criticism of Trump is still verboten within the party. “I don't want to play the blame game, because I just don't think it's productive,” said West Virginia GOP chair Josh Holstein. “But I do think that it was more economics than it was anything.” Many GOP chairs praised the president’s ability to bring in new voters to the party and credited him for working to turn those voters out on behalf of other candidates. Still, some said they hope Trump’s generation-defining tenure at the top of the party comes to an end, allowing Republicans to choose the nominee without his influence. “Republicans should embrace whoever we decide we're going to get behind as a new president, and let the Trump era be gone by the time we're in 2028,” said Oklahoma GOP chair Charity Linch. Ben Proto, Connecticut’s GOP chair, said he is focused on what he and the RNC can control ahead of 2028 — and wants to make sure the organization stays neutral. “We shouldn't put our hand on the scale,” he said of the 2028 primaries. “I think Republican primary voters are pretty savvy and pretty smart and can figure out who our best candidate is going into the ’28 election.” Trump still has plenty of defenders. Even some chairs who are bucking Trump’s endorsement of Gruters and backing RNC co-chair KC Crosbie’s challenge to him, like Kentucky chair Robert Benvenuti, think Trump should continue to be heavily involved in 2028. “He won't take a back seat and should not take a back seat,” Benvenuti said. “I think he's been a tremendous leader for our country. … I think his message will still ring true and will be very helpful as we go into 2028.” Samuel Benson, Lauren Fedor and Jason Beeferman contributed to this report.

items.originalTitle: New Democratic governors race to deliver relief on costs
items.author: Samuel Benson and Erin Doherty
items.title: New Democratic governors race to deliver relief on costs
items.summary: PARK CITY, Utah — Cost-of-living concerns fueled Democrats to victory this month. Now they’re preparing to do something about it. As newly elected governors gathered for a job training conference hosted by the National Governors Association, conversations among the Democrat-heavy group often turned to the economic woes in their states — and the necessity to get something done quickly. “What are the things that we can do — not in the first 100 days, but in the first 100 hours — that can start bringing some relief to the American people?” Wes Moore, the National Governors Association chair and Maryland governor, said in an interview with POLITICO. Health care and home costs topped the target list. Several newly elected Democratic governors — Jocelyn Benson in Michigan, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Deb Haaland in New Mexico and Rob Sand in Iowa — plan to take action to lower health costs, ranging from caps on prescription drug prices to expanding Medicaid coverage, within days of taking office. California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra promised to spur affordable housing construction. His Nevada counterpart, Aaron Ford, said he plans to limit corporations purchasing private homes, and is preparing a day-one executive order to task every state agency with “finding ways to put money back in people's pockets.” “You hear people signing executive orders to make things easier for businesses, cut regulations, and make it easier to do business. I think that's cool, that's fine, that's dandy,” Ford said in an interview. “But if you can do it for businesses, you can do it for people, too.” Affordability was, far and away, the top issue for voters this cycle. Results from The POLITICO Poll, conducted just days after the midterm elections, found a 47% plurality of Americans — including 59% of Democratic voters and 41% of Republicans — said affordability and the economy were among the main issues driving their vote. Democrats’ tsunami washed over governors’ mansions across the nation: They won 24 of the 36 governor’s races held this month, flipping red states like Texas, Alaska and Ohio, and will hold 30 of the 50 governorships nationwide next year — the most in three decades. These governors and soon-to-be governors will be buoyed by a boon of Democrats in their statehouses: Democrats won unified control of government in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada and Wisconsin; in North Carolina, Democrats flipped the House for the first time in 16 years and broke Republicans’ supermajority in the Senate. As several inches of snow descended on the Wasatch Front and blanketed the glitzy ski resort in Park City this week, the newly elected governors sheltered inside the NGA’s New Governors Leadership Forum — colloquially called “baby governors’ school.” At the two-day seminar, the incoming state executives and their teams attended seminars and workshops, mingled over hors d'oeuvres and heard from current and former governors on what to expect. Former President Bill Clinton, sitting spread-legged in a Team USA sweater Thursday, dished to a room full of governors on his book recommendations (“The Social Conquest of Earth” by E.O. Wilson), fun facts (“The combined weight of ants on earth exceeds the combined weight of all the people on earth!”) and political predictions (“I think if President Trump gets closer to leaving, he may get more interested in leaving actual legacies in forms other than buildings.”) Clinton, who chaired the NGA when he served as governor of Arkansas, also offered some advice to the newly electeds: “The most important thing is that you and your Cabinet and your office and your organizations out in the state know what your priorities are and know what your progress is.” Governors will face a steep climb to deliver immediate relief to Americans. Economic forces are national and international, and much of the past year’s price spikes, from fuel to food to energy, can be tied to the Iran war. Bottoms said she will immediately begin to prepare Georgia agencies for Medicaid expansion, and expects the state legislature — with Democrats now in control of the state House, while Republicans still control the state Senate — to cooperate. “I do believe this is an issue we will get bipartisan support on,” she told POLITICO. In addition to his Day-One executive order, Ford says he plans to work with the Nevada legislature to sign bills in his first 30 days on expanding free public school meals, lowering the cost of prescription drugs to the Medicaid negotiated price and limiting corporations’ ability to buy private homes. Benson said she has already reached out to the Trump administration about tariffs, which includes a 50% tariff on most Canadian exports and have disproportionately impacted Michiganders. She said she has not yet heard back, but “the point is I have reached out, and I do hope to have that conversation.” She also emphasized her focus on lowering health care costs. “That's life or death for so many families,” Benson said. Megan Messerly and Adam Wren contributed reporting.

items.originalTitle: What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?
items.title: What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?
items.summary: We usually picture mountain building as rock being pushed upward. But deep beneath some mountain belts and volcanic arcs, the opposite can happen: dense rock at the base of the crust can become unstable, break away and sink hundreds of kilometers into the mantle, dragging part of the rigid outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) with it. Seismic images suggest that this process, known as lithospheric dripping, has occurred beneath the central Andes and California's Sierra Nevada.

items.originalTitle: ECT Is a Controversial Treatment of Last Resort. I Wish I’d Gotten It Sooner
items.author: Ted Scheinman
items.title: ECT Is a Controversial Treatment of Last Resort. I Wish I’d Gotten It Sooner
items.summary: —David Wall—Getty Images Electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT, isn’t terribly fashionable. People sometimes get an uneasy look on their faces at the mention of it. The treatment has come a long way since those agonizing scenes in Miloš Forman’s One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest —but I understand why ECT still freaks people out. Electricity is what Victor Frankenstein used to animate his monster; as recently as 2020 , the state used it to execute murderers. Nevertheless, in 2021, I decided to undergo the treatment, allowing an electrical current to induce brain seizures in hopes of relieving my depression, because I had tried everything else and was close to giving up on life completely. Though I’m not a doctor, I knew the well-documented side effects of ECT; most famously, memory loss. As a writer, a musician, and a nostalgist, I cared deeply about preserving my powers of recollection. But by the time I began getting shocked, the thought of losing a little memory was less scary to me than spending another day getting crushed by this long disease. ECT is not a one-time thing. My doctors began me on three sessions a week. The treatments always happened early in the mornings. When other people were on their first cup of coffee, I was watching the anesthesiologist plug his tubes into the IV port in my arm. When the sparrows outside were singing, I was lying on a surgical table as the medical team rubbed a conductive glue onto my temples. It felt like warm honey and was meant to help the electricity penetrate my skull. Then the anesthesiologist would tell me to count backward from 100 as he began the flow of the anesthetic propofol, plus a muscle relaxant, which, between them, would have me laughing and then passing out before I got past 96. I would wake up in a different room nearby, sometimes with a headache, sometimes not, sometimes euphoric, sometimes not. I did this three times in the first week. Each time, I surrendered myself. I tried to have faith, or at least simulate faith, that this odd practice would bring me back to life. The oddest part was when it began to work. It took a lot. A lot of ECT. A lot of patience from my girlfriend at the time. A lot of friends taking turns driving me to appointments. A lot of faith in the strange ritual of voluntarily applying electrical currents through my brain. Because I got so many treatments—around two dozen, twice as many as a typical patient—eventually they took a toll, and I found myself unable to summon certain memories from the previous six months, in some cases longer. Yet I emerged from ECT, and from the depression preceding it, much healthier than I’d been in years. Pretty soon I went from being worried about what I’d lost to being astonished at what I had gained. I could write for an audience again, an ability I’d surrendered to depression long before ECT. I could play music in public again. The crying fits stopped. Some of my lost memories came back. I returned to the world. Still, people are, understandably, pretty shocked when they hear that I embraced ECT. What surprises them even more: that I really, really wish I’d gotten it sooner. In modern American psychiatry, ECT is held explicitly as a treatment of last resort, reserved for the stubbornest of what’s called treatment-resistant depression . That wasn’t always the case. In the earliest days of electroshock, long before muscle relaxants and anesthesia were even in the picture, doctors held ECT as the gold standard, and sometimes as a first-line treatment. Lothar Kalinowsky, a pioneer of ECT in the U.S., said in a 1978 interview that a course of five or six sessions could be effective for depression . As psychopharmacology began to take hold, doctors began prescribing ECT later and later in a given course of depression, if at all, and patients accordingly required longer courses: around eight to ten. Today, according to Harold Sackeim, a foundational figure in modern neuromodulation, now professor of psychiatry at the Medical University of South Carolina, a typical course consists of 10 to 12 treatments. In part because of how long I’d waited for ECT, my own illness required around twice that number. In most cases, before recommending ECT these days, a doctor must deem a patient to have exhausted any possibility of improvement from talk therapy and from psychopharmacology. Most patients who reach the point of electrical necessity will have tried not only multiple selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), but also tricyclic and tetracyclic antidepressants and perhaps a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI). That means months and months of spinning from one prescription to another, waiting for relief that too often doesn’t arrive. Meanwhile, a lot of patients don’t even know to ask for ECT, and doctors can be slow to prescribe it. “What we’ve done is essentially reserve ECT for the more and more resistant patients,” Sackeim tells me. Since my own treatment, I’ve interviewed neurologists and ECT doctors. Each of them has agreed with my thesis that if I’d gotten ECT sooner, I would’ve spent less time in the depths of unlivable depression—one that had lasted for years. They also agree that I would almost certainly have experienced less memory loss. The complicating factor here is that depression itself often hampers memory , and the longer and deeper the depression, the more gaps and blurs a person will experience in their memory, even before receiving ECT. In other words, getting shocked earlier could have required me to undergo fewer treatments, while potentially preserving more of my memory. That might sound counterintuitive. But a lot of things about ECT are counterintuitive. For one thing, most people don’t know that ECT consistently spurs measurable growth in one’s hippocampus, a part of the brain that can literally shrink during sustained periods of depression. What’s more, emerging research suggests that ECT stimulates neurogenesis : the production of new neurons and of the glial cells that support them. Electricity doesn’t merely destroy; it can also create. ECT isn’t for everybody, and its side effects are real. But I will never stop being grateful for it. Five years have now passed since I last encountered those electrodes. In those five years, I’ve gotten married, written a new book , and lived a happier and fuller life than the one that I had accepted for too much of my adulthood. The history of ECT is rife with abuses . But what about those of us who could have lived fuller lives, sooner, through the judicious application of some electricity? I hope the next person who could benefit from the treatment won’t have to wait, as I did, until it’s almost too late. If you or someone you know may be experiencing a mental-health crisis or contemplating suicide, call or text 988. In emergencies, call 911, or seek care from a local hospital or mental health provider.

items.title: The call of the seamount: Two new armored tardigrades described in the Atlantic
items.summary: An international team led by researchers from Senckenberg am Meer in Wilhelmshaven has described two new species of marine tardigrades. The tiny marine organisms were discovered in the sediment of the Senghor Seamount off the coast of Cape Verde. According to the researchers, the discovery underscores the role of undersea mountains as oases of biodiversity. The study, which includes comprehensive taxonomic descriptions of the new species, has been published in the journal "ZooKeys."

items.originalTitle: Trump says recent tech outages are "all separate events"
items.title: Trump says recent tech outages are "all separate events"
items.summary: President Trump's wide-ranging remarks Friday touched on the lingering concerns that tech outages at the FAA, NSA, banks and other companies were part of a coordinated attack. Mr. Trump denied that, saying all the incidents were unrelated. CBS News national security contributor Joseph Zacks has more.

items.originalTitle: Federal jury convicts man of starting deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
items.author: Jaimie Ding, Associated Press
items.title: Federal jury convicts man of starting deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
items.summary: The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

items.originalTitle: The Cozy Radicalism of DIY Repair Cafés
items.author: Johnny Kauffman
items.title: The Cozy Radicalism of DIY Repair Cafés
items.summary: This story was originally published by Grist and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk. Some carried broken lamps, glitching electronics, or cracked furniture. Others walked in with tool boxes, multimeters for testing electric currents, and cans of WD-40. Beneath extension cords dangling from the rafters, they sorted themselves into smaller groups: the volunteer electricians, tailors, luthiers, carpenters, and at least one cutler (knife sharpener), commandeering nearby worktables and passersby as needed. That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp. “This is so interesting,” a giddy Pettus said, inspecting for the first time the joints, one of them broken, that held together the chair she’d owned for decades. “You never even know how furniture is put together.” “When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely.” This is Decatur’s semi-regular repair café, one of a few hundred meetings like it across the United States. More Americans than ever are turning to these community gatherings to fix what they already own, resisting the influence of companies selling everything from hiking boots, smartphones, and hot water boilers, that push for replacement over repair. One consequence of this throw-away economy is an increase in greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing that threatens to intensify climate change. Yet, organizers and volunteers consider repair cafés as more than a relatively small climate solution. As inflation rises and wages stagnate, the meetups connect people to a movement with the ambitious goal of changing the fundamentals of America’s consumer economy. At the Decatur repair café, volunteers, wearing green shirts with “I can probably fix that” printed on the back, offered their skills free of charge as patrons observed. A young father of a toddler and squirmy baby watched as a volunteer replaced a switch on a favorite mid-century modern lamp worn out by the older child’s repeated clicking. Murmurs of excitement rippled around the building as the acrid smell of a spot welding project wafted through. Volunteers at the Collier Heights’ repair café examine a broken air fryer. Johnny Kauffman/Grist Pettus’ broken chair held in its wood her family’s story. Soon after she and her husband were married in 1996, they began a search for a dining room set. Pettus wanted the chairs to be comfortable for her entire family, but one of her brothers is nearly 7 feet tall, and another just a few inches shorter. “We are not a tiny family,” Pettus said. “We are a big family.” The newlyweds settled on a simple table and six chair —two “host style” with arms, four without—from the local Ethan Allen store. The furniture came to feel more like home than the many houses where Pettus, her husband, and their children lived. They moved the table and chairs with them from Florida to Connecticut, then to Indiana, Michigan, Texas, and finally to Georgia. “ I don’t know anyone’s chairs that I like more than my own,” Pettus said. “ I feel for the objects around me. I feel sorry for them if they’re broken… I want to make repairing a normal thing.” But after absorbing shakes of laughter during countless games of Hearts, and fidgets of anxiety at family meetings about upcoming moves, one of the chair’s joints finally cracked. “We had the chair just sitting in the corner,” Pettus said, “but no one actually sat in it.” She didn’t know how to fix the chair, but if she sent it to a landfill that would mean trashing a reminder of her fondest memories from the last 30 years. Pettus also thought of one of her children who’d interned at the Environmental Protection Agency and shared his concerns with Pettus about pollution and climate change. Then, after months of the broken chair cluttering the family’s house, Pettus was running Saturday morning errands when she passed the Decatur repair café. She drove the half-mile home to grab the chair, and decided to give it a second chance. “When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely,” said Martine Postma, director of Repair Café International, a Netherlands-based network of 4,000 cafés. “ It’s easier to just go on the internet and order a new item which will come to your doorstep in 24 hours, but that’s also a very lonely, disconnected activity.” Postma, a former journalist with the demeanor of an unflappable librarian, founded her organization in 2010 after the birth of her second child magnified her fears about the planet’s future. “Markets are flooded with trash—with cheap products that we don’t need and that do not work,” Postma said. “They break, and they contribute nothing to our well-being. They just contribute waste.” Repair cafés appear to be inspiring people to use their stuff longer. In 2025, they prevented nearly 2 million pounds of waste—the equivalent of more than 100 fully loaded Boeing 747 aircraft—according to Repair Café International, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to the average consumption of about 1,000 Dutch families. Postma, Pettus, and millions of others often smack into obstacles when they try to fix their own stuff. Broken products are increasingly difficult to repair, according to a report from the Federal Trade Commission titled “Nixing the Fix.” The report details how Americans are incentivized to “replace products before the end of their useful lives” by companies that decide to make repairs less safe, limit the availability of parts, lock software and firmware, or even “disparage” independent repair. In 2023, California, Colorado, Minnesota, and New York passed “right to repair” legislation meant to encourage repair over replacement. A year later the European Union passed a similar directive. Postma and other organizers consider the cafés a natural place for activism to push for right-to-repair measures, although Postma hopes for more sweeping changes in Europe, like a tax on raw materials. She argued it would limit emissions and bolster repair shops, even if it increases the cost of products. “ I feel for the objects around me. I feel sorry for them if they’re broken,” she said.“I want to make repairing a normal thing in everyday life once more.” “If the world ends, at least I’ll know how to fix a motor.” According to Postma, repairing goods is more common in relatively poor countries where replacing them can be especially difficult and expensive. It’s in wealthy countries that repair cafés are thriving, but they’re not at all uniform. Each reflects the surrounding area and its socioeconomics. On a Sunday afternoon in the Collier Heights neighborhood of Atlanta, volunteers brought most of their own tools to the basement of a building owned by a Seventh Day Adventist Church, setting them on white plastic folding tables atop a light pink carpet. The café looked much different from the one a 30-minute drive across the city in Decatur. The median annual household income in the mostly Black Collier Heights neighborhood is roughly $40,000 lower than in Decatur. Many people who brought items wanted them fixed less for sentimental reasons, and more so they could keep using them. Gale Pines walked in with a red air fryer that stopped working after they used it to dehydrate ginger. When their oven ran, Pines said, it heated the entire kitchen. So, while in nursing school, they cooked many of their evening meals in the air fryer, most often chicken nuggets and fries. Pines recently graduated, but had trouble finding a job and couldn’t afford to buy a new $100 air fryer. “It’s just hard to exist,” Pines said. “I don’t really have a very big support network outside of my friends.” One of Pines’ housemates told them about Collier Heights’ repair café. They keep a bag of broken electronics in the garage that they’d prefer not to send to a landfill. “Being in the height of climate collapse we can’t just keep buying new stuff all the time, both for the economy and for our material scarcity,” Pines said. When a volunteer at the Collier Heights repair café opened up the airfryer, they quickly discovered the problem: a bad capacitor. Another volunteer had brought a replacement part, and the two of them made the fix as Pines watched, impressed, but unable to follow the relatively complex repair. Pines felt OK that they hadn’t learned how to fix the air fryer themself. “ To just be around people that want to help other people with the skills that they have, that’s value that is really important to me, and something that I try to do as well,” Pines said. “If somebody in my community has a question about their medication or something and can’t afford to go to the doctor, I’m happy to answer any questions that people have.” Another volunteer, Lew Lefton, said he thought that the satisfaction humans draw from making and fixing things has largely been lost, but apocalyptic threats like climate change and artificial intelligence have driven many people toward rediscovering more basic, human skills that are key to survival. People who come to a repair café have a different way to view the future, according to Lefton, especially if they learn something or volunteer themselves. “If the world ends” he said, “at least I’ll know how to fix a motor.” Back in Decatur, Pettus left the repair café with a newly sturdy chair. A screw and some glue fixed the crack around the joint, but the chair still needed upholstery work. Someone Pettus met at the café, who had provided one of the sets of hands that held her chair together as the glue set, advised her on where to buy fabric. Pettus thought she might bring the chair back to the repair café for help reupholstering its seat cushion. “The beauty of it,” Pettus said, “was that I actually was able to learn more about the chair. It was a great experience to know that—I’m not gonna say I birthed it, I of course did not—but I actually had something to do with helping to get it put back together.”
